summary: The Great Irish Famine of 1845-1852, in which a potato blight became mass death because British governments, absentee landlords and free-market officials like Charles Trevelyan kept exporting food and evicting tenants.

evidence.note: Henry VIII's surrender-and-regrant policy opens the long colonial land story leading to the famine
absentee landlord and middleman system set up in the 1600s, dispossessing Irish tenants
1798 United Irishmen rebellion and its bloody suppression
extended segment on O'Connell, Catholic emancipation and the repeal mass meetings
blight first found in Ireland in 1845, start of the main events
Peel's Indian corn imports and the Corn Laws fight over food policy
biography of Trevelyan, from birth and East India Company career to the Treasury
landlords clearing whole villages in Mayo for sheep grazing at the famine's peak
accounts of evicted families dying, including a dead child's body
famine refugees in Liverpool and anti-Irish press in England
epilogue on the death toll, population loss and Trevelyan's descendant reckoning with him

notes: Primary subject is the famine as an event, so no roles and no lifetime rule; Trevelyan gets a long segment but is secondary. covered_span starts at Henry VIII's 1540s land policy because Part 1 spends a large share tracing the colonial land system as the famine's cause; the brief Norman-era section (1160s) is excluded as background. Genocide framing follows the hosts and Coogan.
